To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the biological methane oxidation in aeration tanks of WWTPs can be promoted by using subsurface bubble aeration instead of surface aeration, by using plug flow instead of completely mixed flow in the aeration tank, by increasing the methane concentration in the wastewater influent and by using methane containing off-gases as aeration source.

the biological conversion of methane in activated sludge tanks should be stimulated by: 1) increasing the aeration rate in the aeration tank, 2) using a subsurface aeration configuration, 3) applying CSTR aeration tank configuration, and 4) using an aeration tank with a higher methane concentration in the influent.

(i) methane oxidation is promoted in activated sludge tanks by high aeration rates and subsurface aeration; (ii) methane oxidation in activated sludge is enhanced when methane concentrations are high; (iii) methane can be oxidized by activated sludge when the tank is aerated by methane containing off-gases, but this process is not efficient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of mathematical models for the simulation and control of wastewater treatment plants, with a focus on biological methane oxidation and its effect on greenhouse gas emissions.
the development of process design tools to reduce the methane emissions of WWTPs.
the biological removal of methane in municipal WWTP's and provides a basis for further research on this topic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
methane oxidation is a promising and cost-effective method to reduce methane emission from WWTPs.
biological methane oxidation is a feasible and effective method to prevent methane emission from municipal WWTPs.
the biological conversion of methane is a promising option to prevent methane emission from wastewater treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

biological methane oxidation in municipal wastewater treatment plants can be stimulated by: (i) aeration with methane containing air, (ii) increasing the methane content in the influent wastewater, (iii) aeration with subsurface bubble aeration and (iv) a CSTR configuration.
methane emissions from municipal WWTPs are mainly determined by process design and operating conditions.
the biological conversion of methane in aeration systems is possible, but the conditions for this conversion should be carefully selected.
The main takeaway from our work is that
methane can be effectively removed in aeration tanks, but that this requires a high degree of aeration.
the design and operation of the activated sludge process should be adapted in order to reduce methane emissions.
the methane oxidizing potential in municipal WWTP can be enhanced by aeration with off-gases that contain dissolved methane.
